subtype: Approach: minimum viable release then iteration [Thinking]
passage: I'm Afreen, a tester on Mohit's team. When the project began I expected a long list of features. Instead Mohit said, "Let's ship a bare login and one report screen within three weeks, and let the users tell us what's next." I thought it looked thin. When I asked why, Mohit said, "If I build everything first, I find out in month six that half of it was wrong. This way I find out in month one." Three weeks later twelve people from the client's office used it. They liked the report, complained that login was slow, and asked for an export button we had never planned. In the review, Mohit put the list on screen and said the second sprint would be those three things, nothing more. I can't tell if Mohit was sure it would work.

qa.q: What did the users ask for that had not been planned?
qa.a: The users asked for an export button that the team had never planned.

qa.q: What did Afreen feel at first about the bare first release?
qa.a: Afreen doubted it and thought it looked thin.

qa.q: What else could Mohit try to gather feedback, and why?
qa.a: Mohit could watch two or three users work with the release in person, because seeing where they hesitate shows things they might not think to report.

qa.q: How might the client's users have felt about being asked what comes next?
qa.a: The users probably felt listened to and more involved, since their comments decided what the second sprint contained.

grounding: Illustrates shipping a minimal login and report screen early and letting user feedback decide what the next sprint contains.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable release then iteration [Thinking]
passage:
Week one. The client wanted twelve features in the new expense app, and Chinmay, leading his first project, felt the weight of all of them. Then he thought: we don't even know which ones they'll use. So he cut the first release to two screens: login, and a single expense report. "Three weeks," he told the team. Gopika raised an eyebrow. "Just that?" "Just that."
Week four. The bare version went live for twenty users in the finance department. Chinmay sat with three of them and watched. Nobody used the fancy filters they'd asked for. Everyone wanted one thing: to take a photo of a receipt instead of typing.
Week five. At sprint planning, Chinmay put the users' comments on the screen. The second sprint was receipt photos, nothing else. Gopika laughed. "That wasn't even in the twelve features." "No," he said. "The users wrote it."

qa.q: How many users got the bare version in week four?
qa.a: Twenty users in the finance department got it.

qa.q: How did Chinmay feel at first about the twelve features?
qa.a: He felt the heavy weight of all of them, which made him question which ones really mattered.

qa.q: What else could Chinmay do after the receipt feature ships?
qa.a: He could watch users again and let their next biggest need decide the third sprint, keeping the same feedback loop.

qa.q: How does the approach look to Gopika?
qa.a: Gopika was doubtful at first but ends up amused and convinced when user feedback reveals a feature nobody had planned.

grounding: Shows a lead shipping a bare login and report screen in three weeks, gathering user feedback and letting it decide the second sprint.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable release then iteration [Thinking]
passage:
"Pema, sit down a minute. You're trying to build every feature before anyone sees anything. Let me, Nilesh, tell you about my first project lead job, when I was twenty-five.
The client gave us a wishlist of fifteen features. I remember thinking, if I build all of it, we'll be done in eight months and they'll hate half of it. I had no idea which half.
So I asked myself: what's the smallest thing that's still useful? A login and one report screen. That's all. We shipped it in three weeks.
Then I watched real users. They ignored my beautiful dashboard. They kept asking to download the report into a spreadsheet.
So sprint two was the download button. Not what I planned. What they needed.
That little release saved us months. Ship the small thing, Pema. Let the users tell you what's next."

qa.q: What did users keep asking for after the first release?
qa.a: They kept asking to download the report into a spreadsheet.

qa.q: How did young Nilesh feel looking at the fifteen-feature wishlist?
qa.a: Nilesh felt worried that building everything would take eight months and leave users unhappy with half of it.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Nilesh's story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Shipping only a login and one report in three weeks was the key choice, because real users then showed what to build next.

qa.q: How might the users have felt when the download button arrived?
qa.a: They likely felt heard and relieved, getting the feature they actually wanted instead of the unused dashboard.

grounding: Shows a lead shipping a bare login and report screen in three weeks, then letting user feedback decide what the second sprint builds.
